troubleshooting.fix: This looks more like **under-recovery** than under-fuelling. Try a proper easier week or a few days fully off; if a week of real rest restores your energy, the lever is programming and sleep, not pre-workout.

troubleshooting.issue: Fixing fuel and water helped, but you still crash mid-session
troubleshooting.fix: Look at **within-session fuel and hydration** — sipping some carbs and fluid through longer sessions — and honestly audit your sleep, which quietly caps energy even when everything else is right.

timeline.what: **Confirm your cause first** (see above), then do the one move that fixes the two most common drivers at once — start a genuine **deload** (cut your training volume by roughly **40-50%** for 5-7 days, keeping some intensity but far less total work) and eat to at least **energy balance** (taking in as much fuel as you burn): more carbohydrate around training, plus protein in the commonly cited range of about **1.6-2.2 g per kg of bodyweight** a day. Aim for **8-9 hours** in bed. This is not going soft — it is when your body actually rebuilds. This is general education, not medical advice.

Expect to feel *worse before better* for a day or two as accumulated fatigue surfaces — this is normal. By the end of the deload week most people notice their **resting heart rate** (your pulse first thing in the morning, before you get up) settling, deeper sleep, and legs that feel less dead. If you feel no different at all, your load may not be the real problem — look hard at sleep debt and life stress.

Reintroduce volume **gradually** — add back on the order of **10% a week**, not all at once — while keeping the extra food and sleep. Soreness should clear within a day or two instead of lingering. Keep one truly easy day and one full rest day each week; **monotony** (every session hard, with no easy ones) is itself a driver.

The honest checkpoint. If you've deloaded, eaten enough, and slept well, a real **rebound** usually shows by now — training feels good again, mood and motivation lift, sleep is solid. If you have *not* clearly rebounded, stop pushing and **screen for a mimic** (a different problem wearing the same mask — see reassess). Continuing to train through this is how under-recovery becomes a months-long hole.

overtraining.working: Sessions start feeling *good* again rather than a grind, and your **resting heart rate** (take it first thing each morning — memory lies, so write it down) drifts back toward your normal. Soreness clears in a day or two instead of hanging around, sleep feels deeper, and appetite and mood lift. You are chasing the trend over one to two weeks, not a single perfect session.
overtraining.reassess: See a doctor — don't just keep deloading — if two weeks of real rest, food, and sleep bring **no rebound**, or if you notice red flags that point past simple under-recovery: unexplained **weight loss**; feeling cold all the time, hair thinning, or periods stopping (possible **low energy availability**, sometimes called **RED-S** — not eating enough to cover your training — or a **thyroid** problem, the gland that sets your energy and metabolism); heavy snoring with daytime exhaustion (possible **sleep apnoea**, where your breathing keeps stopping through the night); a run-down state that followed a **viral illness** and won't lift (possible post-viral fatigue); unusual breathlessness, chest pain or pressure, or a resting pulse that stays high; or sudden severe muscle pain with dark, cola-coloured urine, which needs **urgent** care. A simple blood test (**ferritin and iron**, which flag **anaemia** — low iron that leaves you drained — plus **thyroid**) catches the common mimics that no amount of training tweaks will fix. This is educational, not medical advice.

context.who: Women, especially with lighter or missing periods
context.mod: You are at higher risk of the **low energy availability** route (sometimes called **RED-S**) — eating clean but not *enough* for your training. Periods stopping or going irregular is a warning sign, not a badge — raise it with a doctor early, and prioritise eating more over training less.

Recovery genuinely slows with age — you need **more** rest days and a longer deload for the same work, and back-to-back hard sessions bite harder. Build in easy days deliberately rather than assuming you can train like you did at 25.

context.who: Big life stress right now (work, family, money, exams)
context.mod: Feel overtrained on *easy* training? **Life stress is the real load** — your body can't tell a hard week at work from a hard block of training. Cut training load while the life stressor is high, and treat sleep and downtime as part of the plan, not extras.

context.who: New to hard training, or just ramped up fast
context.mod: This is usually a **too-much-too-soon** load spike, not deep overtraining — it tends to resolve quickly with a short deload. Going forward, add volume gradually (on the order of 10% a week) and keep genuine easy days in your week.

troubleshooting.issue: No rebound after a full two-week deload with more food and sleep
troubleshooting.fix: You're likely not treating the real cause — or there's a **mimic** underneath (a different problem behaving like overtraining). Re-check the causes above (sleep debt and life stress get missed most), and this is the point to see a clinician for a basic blood test (**ferritin and iron, thyroid**) and to rule out sleep apnoea or a post-viral cause. Do not answer a non-rebound by training harder.

troubleshooting.issue: You deloaded but felt worse, not better
troubleshooting.fix: A day or two of feeling flat as fatigue surfaces is normal. If it lasts the whole week, the driver is probably **not training volume** — look at sleep quality and life stress, and check you actually ate *enough* during the deload. A deload without more fuel and sleep only does half the job.

troubleshooting.issue: You feel wrecked even though your training is genuinely easy
troubleshooting.fix: This points away from training load and toward **life stress** (the total load your body is carrying) or under-fuelling. Stacking on more rest days won't fix a stress or energy problem — address the life stressor and your total food intake, and reassess your sleep.

troubleshooting.issue: Soreness and dead legs that last many days after big sessions
troubleshooting.fix: That's the **inflammation and muscle-damage** route — space your hardest sessions further apart, protect protein and sleep for repair, and avoid piling on another hard session while still sore. If soreness is ever severe with dark, cola-coloured urine or a swollen limb, treat that as urgent and see a doctor.
